papers.title: Fecal Immunochemical Test Outreach for Colorectal Cancer Screening in Community Health Centers: A Randomized Clinical Trial
papers.authors: Martinez M, Roesch S, Largaespada V, Nodora J, Rabin B, Castañeda S
papers.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Colorectal cancer (CRC) screening is suboptimal among people in traditionally underserved populations, many of whom receive primary care at federally qualified health centers (FQHCs). Mailed fecal immunochemical test (FIT) outreach improves screening, especially in underserved populations, but questions remain about impact over time.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effectiveness of centralized annual mailed FIT outreach delivered over 3 years to increase CRC screening in FQHCs.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted between June 1, 2021, and May 31, 2024. Sixteen clinics from 2 FQHCs in Southern California were randomly assigned to mailed FIT outreach or usual care for patients aged 50 to 75 years and not up to date with screening.
INTERVENTION: Intervention components followed best practices for mailed FIT outreach and included educational primers, FIT kits, and telephone reminders.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was the proportion of individuals up to date with any CRC screening after 3 years of intervention (point prevalence); screening at 2 years was a secondary outcome. Due to a resource constraint-related protocol modification, mailed FIT outreach began earlier in year 3, such that some individuals who completed screening in year 2 were not yet due for repeat FIT.
RESULTS: Among 16 clinics serving 20 250 patients, 6 clinics serving 8334 individuals at baseline (4435 aged 55-64 years [53.2%]; 4896 female [58.7%]; 341 Asian [4.1%], 238 Black [2.9%], 2390 Hispanic [28.7%], and 4371 non-Hispanic White [52.4%]) were randomized to intervention and 10 clinics serving 11 916 individuals at baseline (6443 aged 55-64 years [54.1%]; 7250 female [60.8%]; 699 Asian [5.9%], 355 Black [3.0%], 4635 Hispanic [38.9%], and 4436 non-Hispanic White [37.2%]) were randomized to usual care. At year 3, screening was 39.4% (95% CI, 36.3% to 42.6%) in intervention clinics vs 36.5% (95% CI, 31.2% to 42.2%) in usual care clinics, which was not a statistically significant difference (2.9 percentage points; 95% CI, -3.2 to 9.0 percentage points). At year 2, screening was 37.8% (95% CI, 35.2% to 40.4%) in intervention clinics vs 27.0% (95% CI, 21.8% to 32.9%) in usual care clinics (difference, 10.8 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.9 to 16.7 percentage points).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: This study's findings suggest that centralized mailed FIT outreach could increase CRC screening in FQHCs serving populations with persistent disparities, although maintaining intervention fidelity and providing ongoing implementation support over time are needed for consistent impact.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04941300.

papers.title: Dual therapy with tofacitinib and steroids for acute severe ulcerative colitis: a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial
papers.authors: Arora U, Verma M, Madan D, Singh M, Kandasamy D, Narang H
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: One-third of patients with acute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC) fail intravenous corticosteroids. We evaluated whether adding tofacitinib to corticosteroids reduces treatment failure in ASUC.
METHODS: In this single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adults with ASUC were randomized 1:1 to tofacitinib (10 mg three times daily for 3 days, then twice daily) or placebo for 5 days alongside corticosteroids. Primary outcome was treatment failure at day 6 (<3-point Lichtiger reduction or total score ≥10, or colectomy). Secondary outcomes were relapse (≥3-point rise with total ≥10), rescue therapy, and colectomy at 90 days. Modified intention-to-treat analysis was performed. (CTRI/2022/11/047186).
RESULTS: Of 62 randomized patients, 58 were analyzed: 33 in the tofacitinib arm and 25 in the placebo arm. The trial was terminated early because of slow recruitment and did not reach the planned sample size of 98. Day 6 treatment failure was numerically lower with tofacitinib in unadjusted analysis (24.2% vs 36.0%; RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.30-1.51; P = .33) and significantly lower after adjustment for baseline covariate imbalance (adjusted RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.24-0.93; P = .03). At 90 days, colectomy rates were similar (12.1% vs 12.0%; P = 1.0), but more tofacitinib-treated patients remained on assigned therapy (84.4% vs 54.2%) and rescue therapy was lower (HR 0.27, 95% CI 0.09-0.78; P = .01). Serious adverse events occurred in one versus three patients. No deaths occurred with tofacitinib versus two deaths with placebo.
CONCLUSION: Dual therapy with tofacitinib and steroids in ASUC did not significantly reduce treatment failure at day 6, unless adjustment for baseline imbalance in serum albumin was taken into account. It reduced the need for rescue therapy over 90 days without affecting colectomy risk. Larger clinical trials are required to confirm these findings.

papers.title: The effect of telephone-based education and counselling on stoma adjustment and complication severity in individuals with a colostomy: a randomised controlled trial
papers.journal_full: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer
papers.authors: Yurtseven Ş, Deniz Doğan S, Akıl Y
papers.abstract:
AIM: This study aimed to evaluate the effect of telephone-based education and counselling on stoma adjustment and complication severity in individuals with a colostomy.
METHODS: A randomised controlled trial was conducted with patients assigned to the telephone-based education and counselling group (education group) or the control group receiving routine stoma care. Data were collected over a three-month follow-up period using validated measures of stoma adjustment and complication severity.
RESULTS: Baseline characteristics were comparable between the groups. At three months, the education group had significantly higher acceptance and total stoma adjustment scores and significantly lower complication severity scores than the control group. No significant between-group differences were found in anxious preoccupation, social engagement, or anger scores.
CONCLUSION: At three months, participants receiving telephone-based education and counselling had higher stoma adjustment scores and lower complication severity scores than those receiving routine care. Integrating structured nurse-led telephone follow-up into routine practice may strengthen continuity of post-discharge care.

papers.title: Feasibility and safety of an exercise-based prehabilitation intervention before cancer surgery: a pilot randomised controlled trial
papers.journal_full: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer
papers.authors: Hennessy D, Shee A, Rawstorn J, Evans L, Brown S, Wallen M
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: The study aimed to assess the feasibility and safety of an exercise-based prehabilitation intervention and explore preliminary clinical outcomes in breast, colorectal, and prostate cancer patients awaiting surgery in a large regional healthcare service.
METHODS: Patients with breast, prostate, or colorectal cancer scheduled for surgery were recruited at a single study centre and randomised (1:1) to prehabilitation or usual care. The intervention involved supervised aerobic exercise training 2-3 days per week before surgery. Usual care involved standard cancer treatment. Feasibility was assessed through recruitment, attendance, adherence, and attrition rates. Safety was evaluated via adverse event monitoring. Exploratory analyses evaluated group-by-time changes in cardiorespiratory fitness, health-related quality of life, and fatigue from baseline to the pre-surgery and post-surgery assessment timepoints, with 30-day post-operative outcomes (complications and length of stay) also collected.
RESULTS: Of 47 potentially eligible patients approached and screened, 23 were recruited and randomised, and completed baseline assessments. Twenty participants (prehabilitation n = 11, usual care n = 9) completed the pre- and T1 and T2 assessments. Participants attended an average of 5.25 ± 2.16 prehabilitation sessions. Attendance, adherence, completeness, and attrition rates were 91.3%, 82.6%, 85.7%, and 13%, respectively. Five adverse events were recorded in the prehabilitation group (fatigue, n = 3; muscular pain in the extremities, n = 2); all were grade 1. No significant group-by-time interactions were observed for cardiorespiratory fitness, health-related quality of life, or fatigue.
CONCLUSIONS: Among participants who commenced prehabilitation, attendance, adherence, and completeness were 91.3%, 82.6%, and 85.7%, respectively. No serious adverse events were observed. Exploratory clinical outcome estimates were imprecise and did not support firm conclusions regarding intervention effectiveness. Recruitment limitations and the small heterogeneous sample also preclude broader conclusions regarding feasibility.

papers.title: Protective effect of N-acetylcysteine on oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy in colorectal cancer: a randomized controlled trial
papers.authors: Hegazy Z, Tawfik S, Elmashad N
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: Oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy (OIPN) is a dose-limiting adverse effect of FOLFOX chemotherapy in colorectal cancer (CRC) patients. We aimed to evaluate the protective effect of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) against OIPN. Additionally, we investigated its mechanistic effects on serum biomarkers including total antioxidant capacity (TAC), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and neurotensin.
METHODS: Forty-six patients with stage III or high-risk stage II CRC receiving adjuvant modified FOLFOX-6 chemotherapy were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either oral NAC 1200 mg (effervescent tablets or granules) or placebo one hour before each oxaliplatin infusion for four cycles. Serum levels of TAC, IL-6, and neurotensin were measured before and after treatment. Neuropathy was assessed using the FACT/GOG-NTX-12 and NCI-CTCAE scales, and pain was estimated by using the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form.
RESULTS: Neurotensin was significantly decreased in the NAC group compared to controls after treatment (P < 0.001), and was significantly lower post-treatment versus pre-treatment in the NAC group (P = 0.001). IL-6 was significantly reduced in the NAC group versus controls after treatment (P < 0.001), and significantly decreased post-treatment in both groups (P < 0.05). FACT/GOG-NTX-12 and NCI-CTCAE scores were significantly lower in the NAC group at the end of the first two cycles and at the end of treatment (P < 0.05). Pain interference, but not pain severity, was significantly reduced in the NAC group at both time points (P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: NAC administration during FOLFOX chemotherapy significantly reduced OIPN severity, pain interference, and serum levels of IL-6 and neurotensin, suggesting both clinical and mechanistic neuroprotective effects.
CLINICAL REGISTRATION: The study was is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT07391163).

papers.title: Technical overview and clinical outcomes of transabdominal strategies to eliminate or neutralize staple-line intersection during low anterior resection: a systematic review
papers.authors: Annicchiarico A, Gravante G, Melcarne R, Vincenti L, Picciariello A
papers.abstract:
AIM: To systematically classify and describe transabdominal surgical techniques designed to eliminate or neutralize staple-line intersection during low anterior resection (LAR), and to summarize their reported clinical outcomes.
METHODS: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261368367). Major databases were searched for studies describing transabdominal techniques aimed at eliminating or neutralizing staple-line intersection in colorectal anastomosis during LAR. Both modified double-stapling techniques (mDST) and abdominal single-stapled techniques (aSST) were included. Outcomes of interest included anastomotic leak (AL), use of protective stoma, and perioperative variables. Reported outcomes were descriptively summarized, and exploratory aggregated analyses were performed when appropriate.
RESULTS: Seventeen studies (998 patients) were included. Ten studies (529 patients) evaluated mDST (suture-based: n = 192; invagination-based: n = 337), while seven studies (469 patients) assessed aSST. Reported AL rates remained low across both mDST subgroups (3.1% suture-based vs 3.9% invagination-based), with an aggregated rate of 3.6%. The aSST group showed a leak rate of 6.0%. Protective stomas were used in 6.2% of mDST and 33.1% of aSST. Neoadjuvant therapy was used in 20.7% of aSST and 11.9% of mDST. Considerable heterogeneity in study design, technique, and outcome reporting was observed.
CONCLUSIONS: Transabdominal techniques that eliminate or neutralize staple-line intersection appear feasible and associated with low anastomotic leak rates. Modified DST techniques appear technically feasible and have been associated with low reported leak rates. However, owing to the heterogeneity of the available evidence, comparative findings should be considered exploratory.

papers.title: Biomarkers and future directions for immunotherapy in microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer: a systematic review
papers.authors: Xu J, Ni C, Wang P, Qin L
papers.abstract:
The mechanisms of resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in microsatellite-stable (MSS) colorectal cancer (CRC) have 3 interconnected levels, which provide information to guide different biomarker strategies. There is a critical clinical need, as objective response rates continue to be < 10%. We suggest a biomarker stratification model on the basis of clinical actionability. POLE/POLD1 mutations, recommended by the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology for Colon Cancer (Version 1.2025), represent true genomic "hard" indicators. While the benefit of ICI-containing combination regimens was predicted by the Immunoscore-IC in the AtezoTRIBE trial, the ANICCA-class II study recently questioned the value of anti-PD-1 monotherapy. Defects in homologous recombination repair HRR), ctDNA kinetics and subtyping of CMS1 show promise but need to be prospectively validated. TMB, however, has shown no consistent value as a single biomarker, and MSIs, such as transcriptomic signatures or PD-L1 combined positive scores, have not been proven to be useful. Future prospects involve multiomics algorithms that integrate immune profiling and stromal determinants, liver-directed sensitizing approaches and serial ctDNA monitoring of acquired resistance as viable strategies for further patient selection. These data collectively pave the way toward moving away from the "cold tumor" paradigm and toward dynamic, host-integrated testing for precision immunotherapy in MSS CRC.
There are three levels of resistance to ICIs in MSS CRC: intrinsic defects, microenvironmental barriers and metastatic immune privilege, and each has different biomarker implications. We suggest a clinically actionable stratification. POLE/POLD1 mutations are genomic “hard” markers per the NCCN. The immunoscore-IC can predict combination but not monotherapy benefits. HRR defects, ctDNA kinetics, and CMS1 subtyping require prospective validation. The TMB, MSI-like signature, and PD-L1 CPS do not have consistent values. Innovations include multiomics integration, liver-targeting sensitization, and ctDNA resistance monitoring. These results suggest that the need for a single marker should be replaced with host-integrated, dynamic approaches for precision immunotherapy.

papers.title: Analysing the implementation and transferability of an enhanced care pathway integrating systematic supportive cancer care and patient-partner support for people living with anal cancer: Protocol for a mixed-methods study in two French cancer centres
papers.authors: Carillon S, Faure R, Del Rio M, Lemanski C, Tyran M, de Montgolfier S
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Supportive cancer care (SCC) is essential for comprehensive oncology care. It addresses treatment-related adverse effects, reduces long-term sequelae and improves patients' quality of life. Patient-partner (PP) programmes positively impact psychological well-being, patient empowerment and supportive care. Nevertheless, access to SCC remains inconsistent, fragmented and unequally distributed, while PPs are rarely integrated into routine cancer care pathways. Anal cancer is a predominantly localised cancer with high survival rates. Treatment is associated with acute toxicity and often severe long-term sequelae. This interventional public health research study aims to implement and evaluate an innovative enhanced care pathway combining systematic SCC and structured PP support for all individuals diagnosed with anal cancer living in France. The study will assess the intervention's clinical, organisational, and social effects, and will identify the conditions required for its long-term sustainability and transferability.
METHODS AND DESIGN: This is a longitudinal mixed-methods case study conducted in two French Comprehensive Cancer Centres. The intervention entails introducing a systematic, coordinated, and repeated SCC offer together with a structured PP support programme for all patients diagnosed with anal cancer and over 12 months following diagnosis. One centre will implement the enhanced care pathway, while the other will initially provide standard care before progressively adopting the intervention during the transferability phase. Quantitative data will include patient-reported outcomes, clinical information and implementation indicators. Qualitative data exploring implementation processes, organisational changes and contextual determinants, will be collected through observations, semi-structured interviews, focus groups and PP activity logs.
DISCUSSION: The study's results will provide essential scientific knowledge on the implementation of programmes providing equitable SCC and PP support access to people living with anal cancer. Specifically, by combining implementation research, participatory approaches and mixed-methods evaluation, the project aims to identify the organisational conditions for the sustainable implementation of such programmes for this population, and their successful transferability to other populations living with cancer and to other healthcare settings.

papers.title: Is hemorrhoidal surgery really unsafe in inflammatory bowel disease? Results from the HEAD-IBD multicenter study on behalf of IG-IBD
papers.authors: Felice C, Pugliese D, Gallo G, Di Tanna G, Ascolani M, Sica G
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Surgical management of hemorrhoidal disease (HD) in patients with IBD remains controversial because of concerns about impaired outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the safety and IBD-related outcomes of surgical treatments for HD in patients with IBD and to explore factors potentially associated with postoperative complications and IBD flare.
METHODS: HEAD-IBD is a retrospective cohort study promoted by the Italian Group for the study of IBD (IG-IBD). Adults with established ulcerative colitis (UC) or Crohn's disease (CD) who underwent surgery for HD between 2004 and 2024 and had at least 12 months of follow-up were included. Surgical techniques, 1-, 6-, and 12-month complications, IBD flares (6 months), new onset perianal disease, and continence outcomes were analyzed.
RESULTS: A total of 38 patients were included (21 UC, 17 CD), 55% male. Clinically active disease at the last gastroenterology visit prior to surgery was present in 24% of UC and 41% of patients with CD. Open excisional hemorrhoidectomy was the most frequently performed procedure in both groups (66% UC, 73% CD), while non-excisional techniques were used in approximately one-third of cases. No 30-day or 6-month surgical complications occurred in patients with CD. Postoperative surgical complications were observed exclusively in patients with UC (5/21, 24%) and were mostly mild. Within 6 months after surgery, IBD flares occurred in 6 patients (16%), proportionally comparable between CD and UC. During overall follow-up, new-onset perianal disease developed in 5 patients (13%), predominantly in CD (4/5 cases), while new-onset incontinence was observed in 2 (5%) patients, both managed conservatively.
CONCLUSIONS: In this largest European multicenter cohort, surgical treatment of HD in IBD was associated with low morbidity and preservation of anorectal function. These findings support a more individualized approach and underscore the need for prospective studies.

papers.title: Development of a Novel Real-Time Computer-Assisted Colonoscopy Diagnostic Tool for Colorectal Neoplasia and Cancer to Enable Personalized Patient Management: Protocol for a Multicenter Proof-of-Concept Study
papers.authors: Olabintan O, Brunori A, Halvorsen N, Andersen N, Zubiaurre V, Mirzaei M
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Accurate real-time classification of colorectal polyps during colonoscopy is essential for risk stratification, therapeutic decision-making, and surveillance planning, with important implications for colorectal cancer prevention, health care costs, and patient burden. Despite advances in optical diagnosis techniques, including virtual chromoendoscopy and magnification, widespread adoption remains limited because of high operator dependency and variable diagnostic accuracy. Existing computer-assisted diagnosis (CADx) systems predominantly provide binary classification of colorectal lesions, thereby constraining their clinical utility for nuanced endoscopic decision-making.
OBJECTIVE: This study aims to develop and validate a real-time, multiclass AI-based CADx system capable of classifying colorectal lesions into 5 categories: nonneoplastic lesions, low-grade adenomas, high-grade adenomas, sessile serrated lesions (SSL), and invasive colorectal cancer.
METHODS: This multicenter international study consists of 2 phases: model development and proof-of-concept validation. During the model development phase, a large, diverse dataset of >17,000 deidentified endoscopic images and video frames will be prospectively collected from 8 European centers and 1 Japanese center, capturing a broad spectrum of lesion types and patient demographics. A semisupervised learning framework using contrastive representation learning (SimCLR [simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations]) will be used to leverage both labeled and unlabeled data, enhancing feature extraction and classification performance. Expert consensus annotation will be used for labeled data. Lesion localization will be supported by an integrated computer-assisted detection (CADe) module, while model interpretability will be facilitated through gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM). Proof-of-concept validation will be conducted using 250 previously unseen lesion images that will be independently assessed by expert endoscopists. The primary outcome is multiclass diagnostic accuracy, with a predefined target accuracy threshold of 85%, alongside sensitivity and specificity for invasive cancer detection. Secondary outcomes include interobserver agreement, performance across demographic and lesion subgroups, and a qualitative analysis of misclassification patterns. All data will be securely managed within a REDCap database, with strict deidentification protocols and plans to generate an open-access research resource.
RESULTS: Ethics approval has been obtained at all participating centres. Data transfer agreements have been executed by the majority of collaborating sites, with de-identified polyp images and videos currently being uploaded to a secure central database.
CONCLUSIONS: This study aims to deliver a clinically applicable, real-time multiclass CADx system that extends beyond current binary AI models and supports more granular, personalized endoscopic decision-making. By integrating semisupervised learning, diverse international data, and explainable AI techniques, this approach has the potential to substantially advance the methodological foundations and clinical utility of AI-assisted optical diagnosis in routine colonoscopy, contributing to improved colorectal cancer prevention and patient care.

papers.title: Comparative efficacy and safety of subcutaneous vedolizumab versus other targeted inflammatory bowel therapies in patients with moderate to severe ulcerative colitis: a network meta-analysis update
papers.authors: Jiang J, Wojtowicz A, Uyei J, Jin H, Lindsley K, Sanchirico M
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The growing number of targeted inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) therapies available for the treatment of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis has increased the complexity of treatment decisions for clinicians. Clinical decision-making is further hindered by a paucity of head-to-head clinical trials comparing the relative efficacy and safety of available targeted IBD therapies; however, network meta-analyses (NMAs) can indirectly compare treatments.
METHODS: Networks of evidence were formed from 29 randomized controlled trials of targeted IBD therapies. To address differences in study design, adjustments were made to the treat-through trials in order to mimic a re-randomization design. A Bayesian NMA was conducted with the primary analysis using fixed-effect models to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% credible intervals (CrIs) for efficacy and safety outcomes.
RESULTS: There was no significant difference in the maintenance of clinical response or clinical remission of any targeted IBD therapy relative to vedolizumab 108 mg every 2 weeks (Q2W) subcutaneously (SC), except for adalimumab 40 mg every other week (EOW) SC, which had significantly lower odds (clinical response: OR, 0.36; 95% CrI, 0.17-0.76; clinical remission: OR, 0.35; 95% CrI, 0.16-0.75). The odds of experiencing overall adverse events were significantly higher for patients receiving placebo and treatment regimens for six targeted IBD therapies (adalimumab, etrasimod, golimumab, infliximab, ozanimod, and tofacitinib) than those receiving vedolizumab 108 mg Q2W SC. The odds of serious adverse events were not significantly different between any targeted IBD therapy and vedolizumab 108 mg Q2W SC. The odds of overall infections were significantly higher for those receiving treatment regimens for three targeted IBD therapies (golimumab, ozanimod, and tofacitinib) than those receiving vedolizumab 108 mg Q2W SC; the odds for other treatments were not significantly different.
CONCLUSIONS: The results of this NMA update indicate that vedolizumab SC demonstrates efficacy that is either superior or not significantly different from other targeted IBD therapies, including established biologics and novel oral therapies, and a safety profile that is superior or not significantly different with regard to overall adverse events and overall infections. The efficacy and safety of intravenous vedolizumab is equivalent to that of vedolizumab SC.

papers.title: Engineering extracellular vesicles for inflammatory bowel disease and colitis-associated colorectal cancer: from therapeutic innovation to clinical translation
papers.authors: Huang M, Yuan J, Muro P, Jin T, Mao F, Zhu W
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, is a chronic relapsing inflammatory disorder that increases the risk of colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CAC). Despite major advances in biologics and small-molecule therapies, many patients experience primary or secondary treatment failure, adverse effects, and disease recurrence, underscoring the need for more effective, targeted therapeutic strategies. Extracellular vesicles (EVs), including exosomes, microvesicles, and apoptotic bodies, have emerged as promising nanoscale therapeutic platforms owing to their intrinsic biocompatibility, low immunogenicity, cargo-protective lipid bilayer, and natural ability to mediate intercellular communication. Recent advances in EV engineering have further expanded their therapeutic potential through genetic modification of parental cells, cargo loading, surface functionalization, and hybrid biomaterial systems, enabling enhanced targeting, drug delivery, immune modulation, tissue regeneration, and anti-tumor activity. This review summarizes the biological characteristics of EVs and discusses recent progress in engineering strategies aimed at improving their therapeutic efficacy in IBD and CAC. We critically evaluate current preclinical evidence regarding immunomodulation, restoration of intestinal barrier integrity, regulation of gut microbiota, targeted drug delivery, cancer immunotherapy, and inhibition of metastasis. Finally, we discuss the major translational challenges, including manufacturing standardization, quality control, large-scale production, safety evaluation, regulatory considerations, and future perspectives necessary for successful clinical implementation of engineered EV-based therapies.

papers.title: Gut mycobiome dysbiosis in digestive system cancers: immune remodeling and translational implications
papers.journal_full: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
papers.authors: Ma L, Wang Z, Mao J
papers.abstract: Fungal dysbiosis has been reported in colorectal cancer (CRC), gastric cancer (GC), and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), but evidence strength differs substantially by tumor type and model system. Human CRC studies provide the broadest ecological evidence, including altered fungal community structure and fungal-bacterial networks. Human GC evidence is mainly cross-sectional and identifies Candida albicans as a candidate tissue-associated signal rather than a proven driver. In PDAC, human tissue studies report fungal signals, whereas causal support for Malassezia-mannose-binding lectin (MBL)-complement and fungal IL-33/type 2 immunity derives principally from mouse perturbation models. This narrative review synthesizes cancer-specific observations, fungal sensing, epithelial injury, immune remodeling, cross-kingdom interactions, and translational implications. We emphasize that low fungal biomass, contamination, transient dietary or environmental fungi, non-standardized sequencing, spatial uncertainty, and reverse causation limit interpretation. Fungal detection does not establish viability, colonization, or tumor causation. Clinical translation will require standardized controls, absolute fungal-load measurements, spatial confirmation, longitudinal cohorts, functional validation, and external testing of whether fungal features add value beyond established clinical, bacterial, metabolic, imaging, and immune markers.

papers.title: Macrophage polarization and non-coding RNAs in colorectal cancer progression and metastasis
papers.authors: Nami M, Fattahiyan I, Eini P, Eramian M, Vanan A
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major global health burden, with incidence and mortality rates continuing to rise worldwide. By 2040, CRC cases are projected to reach 3.2 million, driven by complex interactions between genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors. While the molecular mechanisms of CRC have been extensively studied, increasing evidence highlights the critical role of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), and circular RNAs (circRNAs) in regulating tumor progression, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance. Recent research reveals that ncRNAs not only influence tumor cell behavior but also modulate the tumor microenvironment (TME), particularly by regulating tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) polarization. The balance between pro-inflammatory M1 and pro-tumorigenic M2 macrophages profoundly affects CRC progression and treatment response. Dysregulated ncRNAs, such as miR-934, lncRNA RPPH1, and circPLCE1, promote M2 polarization and metastasis via PI3K/AKT, NF-κB, and STAT3 signaling pathways, while others like miR-195-5p and lncRNA GAS5 favor M1 polarization and inhibit tumor growth. These molecules act through diverse mechanisms, including exosomal transfer, ceRNA interactions, and transcriptional regulation, forming intricate communication networks between CRC cells and immune components. Understanding these ncRNA-mediated pathways provides novel opportunities for therapeutic intervention, enhancing immunotherapy efficacy, and improving diagnostic precision through circulating exosomal ncRNA biomarkers. Collectively, targeting ncRNA-regulated macrophage polarization holds promise for developing next-generation precision therapies and advancing immunomodulatory strategies in CRC.

papers.title: Health Literacy and Colorectal Cancer: A Scoping Review Across the Cancer Care Continuum
papers.journal_full: Cancer control : journal of the Moffitt Cancer Center
papers.authors: Tjader N, Waldrup B, Barnard J, Blair C, Kim H, Velazquez-Villarreal E
papers.abstract:
IntroductionHealth literacy is increasingly recognized as a critical determinant of cancer prevention, treatment adherence, and survivorship outcomes. In colorectal cancer (CRC), disparities in health literacy, particularly among ethnic minority and underserved populations, may contribute to reduced screening uptake, suboptimal treatment decisions, and poorer quality of life. Although numerous studies have examined the relationship between health literacy and CRC-related outcomes, the evidence remains fragmented across the CRC care continuum, including screening, treatment, survivorship, communication, and digital health. To address this gap, we conducted a scoping review to comprehensively characterize the current evidence regarding health literacy and CRC outcomes in vulnerable populations.MethodsWe conducted a scoping literature review in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. PubMed was searched between January and March 2025 to identify peer-reviewed studies evaluating the influence of health literacy on CRC-related outcomes. Studies were included if they focused on CRC and assessed measurable associations between health literacy and outcomes related to screening, treatment adherence, survivorship, communication, financial toxicity, or patient-reported outcomes.ResultsThirty-nine studies met inclusion criteria and were included in the review. Across diverse geographic and clinical settings, limited health literacy was consistently associated with lower CRC screening rates, reduced knowledge of screening guidelines, increased fatalistic beliefs, and greater perceived barriers to screening. Among CRC patients, low health literacy was linked to poorer treatment adherence, lower chemotherapy uptake, reduced health-related quality of life (HRQoL), and higher mortality risk, particularly among vulnerable populations.ConclusionsThis scoping review reinforces that health literacy is a significant and modifiable determinant of CRC outcomes and contributes to persistent disparities across the CRC care continuum. Standardized, culturally and linguistically responsive interventions targeting literacy gaps should be prioritized to improve equitable CRC prevention, treatment, and survivorship care.
Understanding health information plays a key role in preventing colorectal cancer, making treatment decisions, and maintaining quality of life after diagnosis. Health literacy refers to a person’s ability to find, understand, and use health information to make informed decisions. When health literacy is limited, people may have more difficulty understanding cancer screening recommendations, treatment options, or follow-up care. In this review, we examined published research on how health literacy affects colorectal cancer outcomes. We reviewed 39 studies that explored the relationship between health literacy and cancer screening, treatment adherence, quality of life, and survival. The studies included patients from a wide range of backgrounds and healthcare settings, with particular attention to underserved communities and racial and ethnic minority groups, including Hispanic/Latino populations. Across studies, lower health literacy was consistently linked to lower rates of colorectal cancer screening and less knowledge about screening guidelines. People with limited health literacy were more likely to experience fear, confusion, or fatalistic beliefs about cancer and to report greater barriers to getting screened. Among individuals diagnosed with colorectal cancer, low health literacy was associated with difficulties following treatment recommendations, lower quality of life, and, in some cases, a higher risk of death. These challenges were often more pronounced among people who also faced language barriers or limited access to healthcare resources. Importantly, several studies showed that targeted strategies can help reduce these gaps. Approaches such as using clear and simple educational materials, providing patient navigators, and engaging communities in culturally relevant ways improved understanding and participation in cancer care. Overall, this review highlights that health literacy is a changeable factor that strongly influences colorectal cancer outcomes.

papers.title: Colorectal cancer surveillance in Lynch syndrome: quality standards, emerging technology and complementary strategies
papers.authors: Castillo-Iturra J, Dekker E, Balaguer F
papers.abstract: Lynch syndrome is the most common hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome, and colonoscopy remains the cornerstone of prevention. However, surveillance is limited by missed lesions, variable procedural quality, accelerated neoplastic progression, and the continued occurrence of post-colonoscopy colorectal cancers. This review examines gene-specific differences in colorectal cancer and adenoma risk, quality standards for surveillance colonoscopy, emerging artificial intelligence technologies, and complementary non-endoscopic strategies. Contemporary studies conducted in expert settings have reported higher adenoma detection rates, reflecting improvements in colonoscopy quality. At the same time, randomized trials have shown no clear additional benefit from computer-aided detection when added to high-quality colonoscopy. Among complementary strategies, fecal immunochemical testing may support prioritization and risk stratification, although its optimal threshold, testing interval, and safety for postponing colonoscopy remain uncertain. In parallel, blood-based biomarkers for cancer prediction remain exploratory. Future progress will depend on wider implementation of quality-assured surveillance and prospective validation of adjunctive tools that can safely guide colonoscopy timing and reduce the occurrence of post-colonoscopy colorectal cancers.

papers.title: Polidocanol foam sclerotherapy for patients with Goligher grade IV hemorrhoidal disease unwilling to undergo surgery: preliminary outcomes from a retrospective study with 6-month follow-up
papers.authors: Gravante G, De Simone V, Picciariello A, Sorge R, Sileri P, Gallo G
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Polidocanol foam (PF) sclerotherapy has shown promising results in low- and intermediate-grade hemorrhoidal disease (HD), but evidence in advanced stages remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate patient-reported outcomes following PF sclerotherapy in patients with Goligher grade IV HD who declined surgical treatment.
METHODS: This retrospective analysis included patients with Goligher grade IV HD that declined hemorrhoidectomy after appropriate counseling and underwent 3% PF sclerotherapy between June and October 2025. Outcomes were assessed using symptom-focused subsets derived from the PROM-HISS and HDSS instruments at baseline, 7 days, 30 days, and 6 months. Primary outcome was the change in scores over time. Secondary outcomes included need for additional treatment, complications, and subsequent surgery.
RESULTS: Fifteen patients were included (mean age 58 ± 11 years; 53.3% male). At 6 months, 66.7% of patients requested no further hemorrhoidal treatment. Significant improvements were observed in both scores across all follow-up timepoints (p < 0.05). Pain, bleeding, and prolapse showed the most consistent reductions. One patient (6.7%) required hemorrhoidectomy within 30 days, four patients (26.7%) a second sclerotherapy session. No major complications were observed.
CONCLUSIONS: In selected patients with Goligher grade IV HD who are unwilling or unfit to undergo surgery, PF sclerotherapy may be associated with short-term symptom improvement and may represent a symptom-oriented minimally invasive option for selected patients unwilling or unfit to undergo surgery.
